A scrimmage is a practice game — a game that looks and feels like the real thing, but officially doesn't count.

Think of it this way: before a cricket team plays a real match, they might hold an internal practice session where players from the same squad split into two sides and play against each other. That practice session — informal, low-stakes, but game-like — is a scrimmage.

The word is used most heavily in American football, but it applies broadly to many sports: basketball, soccer, hockey, rugby, and others.

1. Intra-squad scrimmage
This is when a single team splits itself into two groups and plays against each other. No outsiders involved. The coach sets it up purely for practice. Players can try new strategies, test formations, and get game-like reps without any real pressure or consequences.

2. Inter-squad / practice scrimmage
This is when two separate teams (or two different school/club teams) agree to play a game together that is not officially recorded. It counts for nothing in terms of standings, rankings, or statistics. It's just a dress rehearsal. Both teams benefit from the experience of facing real opponents.

In both cases, the defining feature is the same: it simulates a real game, but the result doesn't matter officially.
The "Line of Scrimmage" — A Special Use in American Football

In American football, there is a very specific and important phrase built from this word: the line of scrimmage.

This refers to an imaginary horizontal line drawn across the football field at the exact spot where the ball sits before each play begins. Both teams — the offense and the defense — line up on opposite sides of this line before every single play. Neither side is allowed to cross it until the play officially starts.

Every time the ball is snapped (handed from the center to the quarterback), a new play begins from the line of scrimmage. If the offense gains yards and the ball moves forward, the line of scrimmage moves forward too — to wherever the ball is now.

So the line of scrimmage is essentially the starting boundary for every play in football. It's not a physical line you can see painted on the field (though TV broadcasts often display it as a colored graphic overlay for viewers); it's a rule-based, imaginary line that resets after every single play.

Outside of sports, "scrimmage" can also mean a rough, confused struggle or fight between a group of people — a minor clash or skirmish. This usage is less common today, but you might encounter it in older writing or literature.

For example, imagine a crowd pushing and shoving near a shop entrance during a sale — that chaotic, messy physical scramble could be described as a scrimmage. It carries the sense of disorder, close physical contact, and competing forces bumping into each other. It's not a full-scale war or brawl — it's messier and more confused than a planned fight, but also smaller in scale than a battle.
What Makes a Scrimmage Different from a Real Game?

This is the most important distinction to lock in:

—ScrimmageReal game
Official result?❌ No✅ Yes
Counts in standings?❌ No✅ Yes
PurposePracticeCompetition
Pressure levelLowHigh

A scrimmage is intentionally consequence-free. Coaches use it to build teamwork, test plays, give new players experience, and assess where the team stands — all without the risk of losing a game that matters.

• "The basketball team held a scrimmage on Thursday to prepare for Saturday's tournament."
    A practice game before the real event.
  • "The quarterback was injured during a pre-season scrimmage."
    Hurt in a practice game, not an official match.
  • "The offense struggled to gain yards past the line of scrimmage."
    They couldn't move the ball forward from where the play started.
  • "There was a brief scrimmage outside the stadium as two rival groups of fans clashed."
    A small, rough struggle (non-sports usage).

A scrimmage is a practice game that mimics real competition but carries no official consequences — and in American football specifically, it also refers to the imaginary line on the field where each play begins.
